questions.question: In supervised instruction fine-tuning of a language model for chatbot behavior, what objective is typically optimized during training?
questions.choice_A: Token-level cross-entropy on the assistant’s reference response given the instruction and prior context (teacher forcing)
questions.choice_B: Maximization of human preference scores via reinforcement learning
questions.choice_C: Minimization of the KL divergence from the pretraining distribution without reference responses
questions.choice_D: Direct optimization of BLEU and ROUGE metrics on validation sets

questions.question: Which data source most directly captures the pragmatic structure of real user–assistant conversations for instruction fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: Synthetic question–answer pairs generated from Wikipedia
questions.choice_B: Human-created multi-turn dialogs collected from consented production logs or curated chat sessions
questions.choice_C: Automatically translated news articles with summaries
questions.choice_D: Mathematical proof corpora with formal annotations

questions.question: In knowledge distillation from a teacher LLM to a student, what is the primary benefit of using soft targets with temperature scaling?
questions.choice_A: They eliminate the need for any human data filtering
questions.choice_B: They guarantee that the student will match the teacher’s exact perplexity
questions.choice_C: They expose relative probabilities over alternatives, guiding the student toward the teacher’s uncertainty structure and decision boundaries
questions.choice_D: They prevent catastrophic forgetting of pretraining knowledge by freezing embeddings

questions.question: Which description best characterizes the Self-Instruct approach to building instruction data?
questions.choice_A: Crowdsourcing domain experts to author gold-standard solutions for a fixed syllabus
questions.choice_B: Using reinforcement learning to explore the instruction space and maximize reward
questions.choice_C: Mining supervised examples from textbooks and converting them into dialogs
questions.choice_D: Bootstrapping from a small set of seed tasks by prompting a capable model to propose new tasks and draft outputs, followed by filtering

questions.question: What is the central motivation for adding RLHF after supervised instruction fine-tuning?
questions.choice_A: To directly optimize model outputs for human preferences and safety constraints that are not captured by likelihood training alone
questions.choice_B: To reduce training compute by removing the need for any labeled data
questions.choice_C: To increase sequence length without changing model behavior
questions.choice_D: To ensure the model exactly replicates the teacher’s outputs token-by-token

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a typical component of an RLHF pipeline for chat models?
questions.choice_A: A supervised policy initialization via instruction fine-tuning
questions.choice_B: A reward model trained to predict the next token in a sequence
questions.choice_C: Preference data where humans rank multiple candidate responses
questions.choice_D: An RL optimizer (e.g., PPO) with a KL penalty to a reference policy

questions.question: How do the objectives of supervised instruction fine-tuning and RLHF typically differ in their effects on behavior?
questions.choice_A: Both primarily push the model to be terse and avoid providing any rationale
questions.choice_B: SFT favors exploration while RLHF encourages imitation of pretraining text
questions.choice_C: SFT imitates labeled responses (style and content), while RLHF shapes responses toward what humans prefer among plausible alternatives
questions.choice_D: SFT maximizes reward signals, while RLHF minimizes cross-entropy loss

questions.question: Why is careful prompt formatting (e.g., explicit system/user/assistant roles and separators) important when training for multi-turn dialog?
questions.choice_A: It reduces model size requirements by 50%
questions.choice_B: It eliminates the need for positional encodings
questions.choice_C: It prevents the model from generating out-of-vocabulary tokens
questions.choice_D: It disambiguates speaker turns and conditions the model on role, context boundaries, and instruction scope

questions.question: What is exposure bias in the context of supervised instruction fine-tuning for dialog models?
questions.choice_A: A mismatch where the model trains under teacher-forced gold responses but generates under its own predictions at inference, causing errors to compound
questions.choice_B: A bias toward including topical content that has appeared frequently online
questions.choice_C: A tendency to reveal training data memoranda verbatim
questions.choice_D: Overfitting to the pretraining objective during RLHF

questions.question: What is a common risk when distilling a smaller student from a larger teacher for instruction following?
questions.choice_A: The student will inevitably surpass the teacher on all tasks
questions.choice_B: The student may inherit the teacher’s stylistic quirks, biases, or hallucinations, reinforcing undesirable behaviors
questions.choice_C: The student cannot be trained with cross-entropy on teacher outputs
questions.choice_D: The student will be unable to condition on multi-turn context

questions.question: Why are pairwise preference judgments commonly used to train reward models for RLHF?
questions.choice_A: They require no human annotators and are fully automated
questions.choice_B: Absolute scoring produces strictly better inter-annotator agreement
questions.choice_C: Humans are typically more consistent at relative comparisons than at assigning calibrated absolute scores, simplifying the learning target
questions.choice_D: They guarantee transitive preferences across all response sets

questions.question: What is the main purpose of including a KL divergence penalty to a reference policy during RLHF optimization (e.g., PPO with a KL term)?
questions.choice_A: To force the policy to ignore the reward model signal
questions.choice_B: To ensure the policy never refuses unsafe requests
questions.choice_C: To improve beam search diversity at inference time
questions.choice_D: To constrain the learned policy from drifting too far from the supervised policy prior, mitigating reward hacking and preserving fluency

questions.question: During multi-turn instruction tuning, why is loss often computed only on assistant turns (and not on user turns)?
questions.choice_A: Because training on user turns would teach the model to imitate users rather than produce helpful assistant responses
questions.choice_B: Because user turns contain no text tokens
questions.choice_C: Because user turns are identical across all examples
questions.choice_D: Because assistant turns are always longer than user turns

questions.question: When mixing datasets from different sources (human dialogs, distillation, self-instruct), what is a key practical step to avoid confusing the model?
questions.choice_A: Always remove all system messages
questions.choice_B: Normalize conversations into a consistent chat template with stable role tags and separators
questions.choice_C: Ensure every example contains an identical number of turns
questions.choice_D: Replace all instructions with multiple-choice formats

questions.question: How does instruction distillation differ from classic knowledge distillation?
questions.choice_A: Instruction distillation does not require teacher outputs
questions.choice_B: Classic knowledge distillation cannot use temperature scaling
questions.choice_C: Instruction distillation targets the teacher’s instruction-following style and response preferences in dialog, whereas classic distillation often matches token distributions more generally across tasks
questions.choice_D: Classic distillation requires RL optimization, while instruction distillation does not

questions.question: Which curation strategy best addresses the trade-off between broad task coverage and depth in supervised instruction datasets?
questions.choice_A: Restricting to a single domain with very long conversations
questions.choice_B: Filtering out all rare or long-tail instructions
questions.choice_C: Only using teacher-forced generations without any negative examples
questions.choice_D: Combining diverse task families with sufficient per-task examples, deduplication, and quality filters to reduce noise

questions.question: After instruction SFT, why might a model still produce unsafe or overly verbose content?
questions.choice_A: SFT imitates observed responses and does not directly encode human preferences or penalties for verbosity/toxicity beyond what appears in the labeled data
questions.choice_B: SFT removes all capabilities learned during pretraining
questions.choice_C: SFT forces the model to ignore formatting tokens
questions.choice_D: SFT trains the model only on user turns

questions.question: What is a lightweight alternative to full RLHF that still uses preference signals to improve responses?
questions.choice_A: Increasing beam width during decoding
questions.choice_B: Rejection sampling: generate multiple candidates from the SFT model, score with a preference/reward model, select top outputs, and further fine-tune on them
questions.choice_C: Dropping the KL penalty during PPO
questions.choice_D: Training solely on synthetic math problems

questions.question: Why are perplexity and next-token accuracy often insufficient to evaluate instruction-following quality post-RLHF?
questions.choice_A: They cannot be computed for long sequences
questions.choice_B: They always correlate negatively with user satisfaction
questions.choice_C: They measure likelihood under a reference distribution rather than alignment with human preferences, safety, or helpfulness
questions.choice_D: They double-count gradients from the reward model

questions.question: When generating model-written instruction–response pairs (e.g., via self-instruct), which practice best mitigates degeneration and distribution shift?
questions.choice_A: Always accepting the first sample from the model
questions.choice_B: Removing all human-authored seed tasks
questions.choice_C: Training the reward model jointly on the same synthetic data
questions.choice_D: Applying filtering, de-duplication, and diversity-promoting sampling; optionally using teacher ensembles and heuristic checks before adding to training
